newsitem.title: ITALY: Alfa Romeo plans for its renaissance.
newsitem.headline: Alfa Romeo plans for its renaissance.

text.p: Alfa Romeo's renaissance has been a long time coming. Bedevilled by poor quality and held back by former state ownership, Italy's famous sports car company has remained in the doldrums for decades.

For Alfa's owners of the last 10 years, giant carmaker Fiat, all is set to change. But never has so much depended on one model, planned for launch this fall, to break the stranglehold of German cars on the sports car sector.
Fiat has been hard at work spending five trillion lire ($3 billion) on Alfa to try to revive its former glories of the 1940s and 1950s.
But even as Fiat has pumped in money, sales of Alfas worldwide have slipped over the last few years.

Alfa is pinning its hopes on a new sports car, the 156, which it forecasts will more than double peak sales of the outgoing ageing 155 and get close to sales of the sector's front runner and benchmark car, the BMW 3-series.
It's a very tall order. Alfa has spent a lot of time applying the finishing touches to this new medium-large car to give it an Italian flair, and with it rests Alfa's future.
"We are ambitious for the 156, and we see it doing well in new markets for us," said Giuseppe Perlo, senior vice president for product at Fiat Auto.

Alfa -- or Anonima Lombarda Fabbrica di Automobili -- was born in 1910 in Milan and the firm's trademark, a red cross and the Visconti snake, comes from one of Milan's most famous historical families.

Neopolitan entrepreneur Nicola Romeo soon took over the company and his name became inextricably linked to the group's fortunes. However, the combined group soon ran into financial problems and was rescued by the Italian state in the 1930s.
Under state-ownership, the firm enjoyed its best years on the race track after World War II, and its entry into the mass market with its much-loved Giulietta model was a great success in the 1950s.

Alfa's problems mounted in the late 1960s with over-ambitious plans for expansion amid political and social difficulties in Italy. The label of poor quality at Alfa is something the company has sought ever since to combat.

A second factory was built at Pomigliano D'Arco, near Naples, in the late 1960s to build a new model, the Alfasud. The first cars rolled out of Pomigliano in 1971. The over ambitious expansion at Pomigliani, along with labour difficulties, led some commentators to call Pomigliano the "worst car factory in western Europe."

The Italian state soon tired of the drain on cash at the money-losing company producing around 220,000 cars a year. In 1987 Fiat stepped in, after Ford Motor Co. had put in an offer, bringing Fiat, Lancia and Alfa all under the same roof.
After the takeover, Alfa's problems continued and despite new models, production fell by half to just over 100,000 by 1994.

Alfa production director Giorgio Pavia said sales were weak over the last five years due a poor Italian market, the relatively unsuccessful medium-large 155 and the fall in sales of the ageing 164, the biggest model in the Alfa range.

In a highly competitive medium/large upscale car market, Alfa hopes the new 156 will sell 86,000 units in 1998 and around 121,000 in 1999 and beyond, pushing total Alfa annual sales back above 200,000 per year.

But there is a lot of tough competition, especially from BMW, Mercedes and Volkswagen's Audi. Still, Alfa's Perlo is upbeat. "We will have two new models in the next few months and then the whole range will have been replaced between October 1994 and the middle of 1998."
Designers have tried to add a certain Latin flair to the 156. The traditional Alfa radiator grill is cut deep into the front bumper, similar to the 1950s Giulietta.
Front door handles revive 1960s chrome, while the rear door handles are hidden in the black plastic trim of the rear windows to give the four-door car the appearance of a two-door coupe.
